p.src: When Tripitaka saw them, he stood respectfully beside the gate and offered a greeting. The monks hurriedly returned his courtesy and said with a smile, “Forgive us for failing to welcome you sooner.” They asked, “Where have you come from? Please come into the abbot’s quarters and take some tea.” Tripitaka replied, “This disciple is an imperial envoy from the Eastern Land, bound for the Thunderclap Monastery to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. As evening is drawing on now that we have reached this place, we wish to lodge at your noble monastery for one night.” The monk said, “Please come inside and be seated. Please come inside and be seated.” Only then did Tripitaka call for Pilgrim to lead the horse inside. When the monk suddenly caught sight of Pilgrim’s features, he grew somewhat frightened and asked, “What sort of creature is that leading the horse?” Tripitaka said, “Speak softly, speak softly. He is quick-tempered; if he hears you call him some sort of creature, he will be angry. He is my disciple.” The monk shuddered, bit his finger, and said, “How could you take such an ugly, monstrous-looking fellow as a disciple?” Tripitaka said, “You cannot tell by looking at him. Ugly he may be, but he is extremely useful.”

p.src: The monk had no choice but to accompany Tripitaka and Pilgrim through the mountain gate. Inside the gate, they saw four large characters inscribed above the main hall: “Guanyin Chan Monastery.” Tripitaka was delighted once more and said, “This disciple has repeatedly received the Bodhisattva’s sacred grace but has not yet had the chance to bow in gratitude. Now that I have encountered this Chan monastery, it is as though I have seen the Bodhisattva herself. How good it will be to bow and give thanks.” Hearing this, the monk immediately ordered an attendant to open the hall and invited Tripitaka to worship. Pilgrim tethered the horse, dropped the luggage, and went up into the hall with Tripitaka. Tripitaka stretched out his back and body, laid his breast flat upon the floor, and kowtowed before the golden image. The monk went to beat the drum. Pilgrim went to strike the bell. Prostrate before the altar, Tripitaka prayed with all his heart. When the prayers and obeisances were complete, the monk stopped drumming, but Pilgrim went on striking the bell without pause, now rapidly, now slowly, for a very long time. The attendant said, “The worship is already over. Why are you still striking the bell?” Only then did Pilgrim drop the bell hammer. He laughed and said, “What would you know about it! I am merely ‘a monk for a day, striking the bell for a day.’” By now the disorderly clanging had alarmed every monk in the monastery, great and small, including the elders of both the upper and lower quarters. They all rushed out together, crying, “What savage is banging the bells and drums so wildly?” Pilgrim sprang out and barked, “It was your grandpa Sun striking it for amusement!” At the sight of him, the monks were so terrified that they tumbled over one another. Prostrate on the ground, they cried, “Lord Thunder!” Pilgrim said, “The Lord of Thunder is my great-great-grandson. Get up, get up! Do not be afraid. We are noble visitors from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land.” Only then did the assembled monks bow in greeting. When they saw Tripitaka, they finally felt reassured and ceased to fear. Among them was the monastery’s prior, who invited them, saying, “My lords, please come to the rear abbot’s quarters and take tea.” They therefore untied the reins and led the horse, shouldered the luggage, passed around the main hall, and went straight into the rear quarters, where everyone took his proper seat.

p.src: The monks said, “The patriarch has come.” Tripitaka bowed to welcome him and said, “Venerable abbot, this disciple offers you his respects.” The old monk returned the courtesy, and they resumed their seats according to rank. The old monk said, “A little while ago, the younger monks told me that noble visitors had come from the Tang court in the Eastern Land, so I came out to pay my respects.” Tripitaka said, “We have presumptuously intruded upon your treasured mountain without knowing what was proper. Forgive us, forgive us.” The old monk said, “Not at all, not at all.” He then asked, “My lord, how far is it from the Eastern Land to here?” Tripitaka replied, “From the border of Chang’an, it is more than five thousand li. After crossing the Mountain of Two Frontiers, I took on this humble disciple. We then traveled through the Western Tibetan country of Hami, journeying for another two months and covering five or six thousand li before at last reaching your honored abode.” The old monk said, “Then it has been a journey of some ten thousand li. This disciple has idled away his whole life without ever passing beyond the monastery gate. Truly I am one who ‘sits in a well and gazes at the sky,’ a useless old piece of rotten wood.” Tripitaka then asked, “Venerable abbot, how advanced is your honored age?” The old monk replied, “I have foolishly lingered on for two hundred and seventy years.” Hearing this, Pilgrim said, “Why, he is still a descendant of mine ten thousand generations removed.” Tripitaka glared at him and said, “Mind your tongue. Do not forget your place and offend our host.” The monk then asked, “My lord, how old are you?” Pilgrim replied, “I dare not say.”

p.src: The old monk took this merely for a mad remark and paid it no heed. He asked no more questions and simply called for tea. One fortunate young attendant brought out a tray of mutton-fat jade bearing three cloisonné teacups inlaid with gold. Another attendant carried a white-copper pot and poured three cups of fragrant tea. Truly, its hue outshone the brilliant pomegranate blossom, and its fragrance surpassed that of the cassia flower. At the sight, Tripitaka praised them without end, saying, “What splendid things! What splendid things! Truly, fine fare in fine vessels.” The old monk said, “They are hardly worthy of your eyes, hardly worthy. My lord comes from the celestial court of a mighty realm and has seen treasures without number. How could such utensils deserve so much praise? Since you come from that exalted country, might you have some treasure you could lend this disciple to admire?” Tripitaka replied, “Alas, my Eastern Land possesses no particular treasures; and even if it did, the road is so long that I could not have brought them with me.” From beside him Pilgrim said, “Master, the other day I saw that cassock in our bundle. Is that not a treasure? Why not take it out and let him see it?” At the mention of a cassock, every one of the monks gave a scornful laugh. Pilgrim said, “What are you laughing at?” The prior said, “My lord has just called a cassock a treasure. That truly is laughable. As for cassocks, even monks such as ourselves own more than twenty or thirty apiece; and our patriarch, who has been a monk here for some two hundred and fifty or sixty years, must possess fully seven or eight hundred.” Pilgrim called, “Bring them out and let us see them.” The old monk too was seized by a sudden desire to show off. He ordered the attendants to open the storeroom and the mendicants to carry out the chests. They brought out twelve chests in all, set them in the courtyard, and unlocked them. Clothes racks were set up on both sides and ropes stretched all around. The cassocks were shaken out one by one and hung up for Tripitaka to inspect. Indeed, the entire hall was filled with splendid embroidery, and all four walls were draped in damask and gauze.

p.src: The Pilgrim examined them one by one. They were all garments adorned with floral brocade, embroidery, and gold thread. He laughed and said, “Fine, fine, fine! Put them away, put them away. Now take ours out and let them see it.” Tripitaka caught hold of the Pilgrim and whispered, “Disciple, do not vie with others in displaying wealth. We are alone and far from home; I fear something may go wrong.” The Pilgrim said, “What could go wrong merely from looking at a cassock?” Tripitaka said, “You do not understand. The ancients said, ‘Rare treasures and precious curios must not be shown to the greedy, treacherous, and deceitful.’ Once such a thing meets their eyes, it is bound to stir their hearts; and once their hearts are stirred, they are bound to devise a scheme. If you fear calamity, you may surrender it when they demand it; otherwise, the loss of life itself may spring from this. It is no small matter.” The Pilgrim said, “Rest easy, rest easy. Old Sun will answer for everything.” Without allowing any further argument, he hurried away and untied the bundle. Rays like sunset clouds were already streaming from it, though the contents were still wrapped in two layers of oiled paper. He removed the paper, took out the cassock, and shook it open. p.src: When the old abbot saw such a treasure, wicked desire duly stirred within him. He stepped forward, knelt before Tripitaka, and said with tears in his eyes, “This disciple of yours is truly without good fortune.” Tripitaka helped him up and asked, “What is it that the venerable abbot wishes to say?” He replied, “When Your Reverence unfolded this treasure just now, it was already late. My eyes are dim with age, and I could not see it clearly. Does that not mean I lack the good fortune to behold it?” Tripitaka said, “Bring lamps, and let him look again.” The old monk said, “Your Reverence’s treasure already shines brilliantly. If lamps are lit as well, the glare will be still more dazzling, and I shall never see it closely.” The Pilgrim asked, “Then how would you like to look at it?” The old monk said, “If Your Reverences would graciously trust me, let this disciple take it to the rear chambers and examine it closely through the night. Tomorrow morning I shall return it before Your Reverences continue westward. What do you think of this request?” Tripitaka was startled by these words and reproached the Pilgrim: “This is all your doing, all your doing!” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “What is there to fear from him? Let me wrap it up and give it to him to examine. If anything goes amiss, Old Sun will set it all to rights.” Unable to restrain him, Tripitaka handed the cassock to the old monk and said, “Take it and examine it as you please. Only return it to me unchanged tomorrow morning, without the slightest damage or stain.” Overjoyed, the old monk ordered the young attendant Xing to carry the cassock inside. He then ordered the monks to sweep the front meditation hall clean, set out two rattan couches with bedding, and invite the two honored guests to rest there; at the same time, he had them prepare a vegetarian breakfast to see the travelers off the next morning. Thereupon they all dispersed. Master and disciple shut the meditation hall and went to sleep, and we shall speak no more of them for now.

p.src: Now the monk, having tricked them out of the cassock, took it to a rear chamber and, beneath the lamplight, wailed and wept bitterly over it. His distress so alarmed the monks of the monastery that none dared go to sleep before him. The young attendant Xing did not know the reason either, so he went and told the monks, “Grandfather has been crying until the second watch, and still he has not stopped.” Two of his favorite grand-disciples came forward and asked, “Grandmaster, why are you weeping?” The old monk replied, “I weep because I lack the good fortune to behold the Tang Monk’s treasure.” The young monk said, “Grandfather, you are so old that your wits have left you. His cassock lies right before you. You need only unwrap it and look. Why must you weep so bitterly?” The old monk said, “I cannot look at it for long enough. I am two hundred and seventy years old this year, yet all I have managed to acquire are a few hundred cassocks. How could I ever obtain one like his? How could I ever become a Tang Monk?” The young monk said, “Grandmaster, you are mistaken. The Tang Monk is merely an itinerant monk who has left his home and native land. At your great age, you have enjoyed comforts enough. Why would you instead wish to resemble him and become an itinerant monk?” The old monk replied, “Though I live comfortably at home and enjoy ease in my declining years, I have no chance to wear his cassock. If only I could wear it for a single day, I could close my eyes content even in death, and feel that my life as a monk in this mortal world had not been in vain.” The monks said, “What nonsense! If you wish to wear his cassock, what difficulty is there? If we keep him here for one more day tomorrow, you can wear it for one day; if we keep him for ten days, you can wear it for ten days. That will settle the matter. Why torment yourself with such bitter weeping?” The old monk said, “Even if we kept him for a whole year, I could wear it only for that year; it still would not last forever. When he wishes to leave, we shall have no choice but to let him take it. How could we keep it for good?”

p.src: As they were speaking, a young monk named Guangzhi stepped forward and said, “Grandfather, if you wish to keep it forever, that is easily done.” Hearing this, the old monk cheered at once and said, “My child, what excellent plan have you?” Guangzhi said, “That Tang Monk and his companion are travelers, utterly exhausted from the road, and by now they are fast asleep. Let us choose several strong men, arm them with spears and swords, break into the meditation hall, and kill the pair. We can bury their bodies in the rear garden, so that only our own household knows. We shall also take their white horse and baggage, while keeping the cassock as a family treasure. Would that not be a lasting provision for our descendants?” At these words the old monk was overjoyed. Only then did he wipe away his tears and say, “Fine, fine, fine! It is an incomparable plan.” They immediately began readying spears and swords.

p.src: But among them was another young monk named Guangmou, Guangzhi’s junior fellow-disciple. He came forward and said, “That plan is no good. If we mean to kill them, we must first judge the circumstances. The pale-faced one seems easy enough, but the hairy-faced one looks difficult. If by any chance we fail to kill him, would we not bring disaster upon ourselves instead? I have a way that requires neither blade nor spear. I wonder what you think of it?” The old monk said, “My child, what method do you have?” Guangmou said, “In this humble grand-disciple’s opinion, we should now summon every branch of the monastery on the eastern hill and order each man to bring a bundle of dry firewood. We shall sacrifice those three meditation halls and set them ablaze, leaving the travelers no way to escape, and burn them together with their horse. Even if the households before and behind the mountain see it, we need only say that the travelers were careless and started a fire that burned down our meditation halls. Would not both monks then be burned to death? It would also serve nicely to conceal the truth from everyone. And would the cassock not become our family treasure?” All the monks were delighted when they heard this, and cried, “Excellent, excellent, excellent! This plan is better still, better still!” They then ordered every branch of the monastery to bring firewood. Alas! This very scheme was destined to bring the long-lived old monk to the end of his allotted span and reduce the Guanyin Monastery to dust. The monastery had some seventy or eighty separate branches, with more than two hundred monks, great and small. That night they all rushed to carry firewood, surrounding the meditation hall on every side, front and rear, until no passage remained. There they made ready to set the fire, and for now we shall speak no more of them.

Would not both monks then be burned to death?
It would also serve nicely to conceal the truth from everyone.
And would the cassock not become our family treasure?”
All the monks were delighted when they heard this, and cried, “Excellent, excellent, excellent! This plan is better still, better still!”
They then ordered every branch of the monastery to bring firewood.
Alas!
This very scheme was destined to bring the long-lived old monk to the end of his allotted span and reduce the Guanyin Monastery to dust.
The monastery had some seventy or eighty separate branches, with more than two hundred monks, great and small.

That night they all rushed to carry firewood, surrounding the meditation hall on every side, front and rear, until no passage remained. There they made ready to set the fire, and for now we shall speak no more of them.

p.src: The splendid Wukong turned a somersault and leapt up inside the Southern Gate of Heaven. Pang, Liu, Gou, and Bi were so terrified that they bowed low, while Ma, Zhao, Wen, and Guan bent their backs, all crying, “This is terrible! This is terrible! The lord who caused havoc in Heaven has come again!” Wukong waved his hand. “Gentlemen, dispense with the courtesies and do not be alarmed. I have come in search of Virupaksha, the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King.” Before he had finished speaking, the Heavenly King arrived and greeted him. “It has been a long time indeed. I heard earlier that the Bodhisattva Guanyin went to see the Jade Emperor and borrowed the Four Duty Gods, the Six Ding and Six Jia Spirits, the Guardians, and others to protect the Tang Monk on his journey west for the scriptures. They said that you had become his disciple. How is it that you have leisure to come here today?” Wukong replied, “There is no time now to speak of old times. The Tang Monk has encountered villains on the road, and they have set fire to burn him. The danger is extreme, so I have come especially to borrow your fireproof cover and save him. Bring it quickly for me to use, and I shall return it at once.” The Heavenly King said, “You are mistaken. If villains have set a fire, you should borrow water to save him. Why do you want the fireproof cover?” Wukong replied, “You do not understand the truth of the matter. If I borrow water to save him, the fire will fail to take hold, and that would only suit those villains; I only want this cover to shield the Tang Monk from harm. As for everything else, let it burn as it may. Hurry, hurry! By now it may already be too late. Do not delay the business I have to attend to below.” The Heavenly King laughed. “This monkey still harbors the same uncharitable thoughts. He cares only for his own people and not for anyone else.” Wukong said, “Hurry, hurry! Stop wagging your tongue, or you will ruin a great affair.” The Heavenly King dared not refuse and handed the cover to Wukong.

p.src: This indeed was a single spark capable of burning ten thousand acres of fields. In moments the wind raged and the fire swelled, until the whole Guanyin Monastery glowed red in every quarter. See how the monks carried chests, lifted trunks, snatched up tables, and bore away cooking pots, filling the whole courtyard with cries of misery. Sun Wukong protected the abbot’s quarters at the rear, while the fireproof cover shielded the meditation hall in front. Everywhere else, before and behind, the flames blazed fiercely: scarlet tongues of fire shone splendidly against the sky, and golden light pierced through the walls.

p.src: Unexpectedly, when the fire broke out, it startled all the beasts and monsters of the mountain. Some twenty li due south of the Guanyin Monastery stood Black Wind Mountain. Within the mountain was a Black Wind Cave, and in that cave lived a demon who had just awakened and was turning over in bed. Seeing light streaming through the window, he assumed that dawn had come. But when he rose to look, he saw that it was the glare of a fire directly to the north. The demon exclaimed in alarm, “Ah! The Guanyin Monastery must be on fire. How very careless those monks are! I shall go and see, and help them put it out.” The fine demon mounted a cloud and instantly arrived beneath the smoke and flames. Sure enough, the fire towered into the sky. The halls in front had all burned hollow, while smoke and fire were just consuming the two side galleries. He strode inside and was just calling for water when he saw that there was no fire in the rear quarters and that someone on the roof ridge was fanning the flames. He at once understood what was happening. Hurrying inside to look, he saw a rosy, many-colored radiance in the abbot’s room and a bundle wrapped in blue felt upon the table. He unwrapped it and found a brocade cassock, a rare treasure of the Buddhist faith. Truly, wealth stirs the human heart. He neither fought the fire nor called for water, but seized the cassock and looted it amid the confusion. Then he wheeled his cloud about and went straight back toward the eastern mountain.

p.src: The fire burned until dawn at the fifth watch before it finally died out. See how the monks, stripped almost naked and weeping bitterly, searched the ashes for copper and iron, raked through charred wood, and groped for gold and silver. Some put up makeshift shelters within the ruined wall enclosures; others propped up cooking pots beside the bare walls and prepared food. Their cries of grievance and their disorderly clamor need not be related.

p.src: Now Wukong took the fireproof cover, turned a somersault up to the Southern Gate of Heaven, and returned it to the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King, saying, “Thank you for the loan, thank you.” The Heavenly King took it and said, “The Great Sage is truly trustworthy. I was just worrying that you might not return my treasure and that I would have nowhere to seek its recovery. What a relief that you have brought it back yourself.” Wukong said, “Do you take old Sun for a man who borrows things through deception to someone’s face? As the saying goes, ‘Return what you borrow in good order, and it will not be hard to borrow again.’” The Heavenly King said, “We have not met for a long time. Why not come into my palace and sit for a while?” Wukong replied, “Old Sun is not as he was before, idling on a worn-out bench and indulging in endless lofty talk. Now that I am protecting the Tang Monk, I have no leisure. We shall talk another time, another time.” He hurriedly took his leave and dropped down on his cloud, just as the sun was rising. He went straight to the front of the meditation hall, shook himself, changed into a little honeybee, and flew inside. When he resumed his true form and looked, his master was still deep asleep.

p.src: Wukong called, “Master, day has broken. Get up.” Only then did Tripitaka awaken. Turning over, he said, “So it has.” He dressed, opened the door, and came out. Looking up suddenly, he saw only crumbling walls of red brick; the towers and halls had vanished. Greatly alarmed, he cried, “Ah! Why have all the buildings disappeared, leaving nothing but red walls?” Wukong said, “You are still dreaming. There was a fire here last night.” “How is it that I knew nothing of it?” asked Tripitaka. Wukong replied, “I guarded the meditation hall. You were sleeping soundly, Master, so I did not disturb you.” Tripitaka said, “If you had the power to protect the meditation hall, why did you not put out the fire in the other buildings?” Wukong laughed. “You should know, Master, that matters happened just as you said yesterday. They coveted our cassock and plotted to burn us to death. Had I not noticed in time, by now we would all be bones and ashes.” Hearing this, Tripitaka asked fearfully, “Was it they who set the fire?” “Who else could it have been?” said Wukong. Tripitaka said, “Could it be that they treated you discourteously and you did this deed yourself?” Wukong said, “Am I such an incorrigible rogue that I would commit so wicked a deed? They truly did set the fire themselves. When I saw how vicious they were, I indeed refused to fight the fire for them. I merely lent the wind a little help.” Tripitaka cried, “Heaven help us! Heaven help us! When a fire breaks out, one should bring water. Why did you instead help the wind?” Wukong said, “Do you not know the old saying: ‘If a man bears no heart to harm a tiger, the tiger bears no intent to harm the man’? Had they not played with fire, why would I have played with the wind?” Tripitaka asked, “Where is the cassock? Surely it has not been burned?” Wukong replied, “It is safe, it is safe. It could not have burned; there was no fire in the abbot’s quarters where the cassock was kept.” Tripitaka said angrily, “I care nothing for your assurances. If it is damaged in the least, I need only recite that formula a few times and you will die.” Wukong grew alarmed. “Master, do not recite it, do not recite it! I promise I will find your cassock and return it to you. Let me go and fetch it, and then we shall be on our way.” Tripitaka then led the horse, while Wukong shouldered the luggage. They left the meditation hall and went straight to the abbot’s quarters at the rear.

p.src: Now while the monks were deep in grief, they suddenly saw master and disciple approaching, one leading the horse and the other carrying the luggage. Every one of them was frightened out of his wits and cried, “Their wronged ghosts have come to claim our lives!” Wukong shouted, “What do you mean by ghosts come to claim your lives? Return my cassock at once!” All the monks dropped to their knees and kowtowed, crying, “Mercy, grandfather! Every wrong has its culprit, and every debt its debtor. If you have come for lives, it has nothing to do with us. Guangmou and the old abbot devised the plot to kill you. Do not demand our lives!” Wukong barked, “You accursed beasts! Who asked you for anyone’s life? Just bring out my cassock, return it to me, and let us go on our way!” Among them, two monks of greater courage said, “My lord, you were burned to death in the meditation hall, yet now you have returned to demand the cassock. Are you truly men, or are you ghosts?” Wukong laughed. “You pack of sinful beasts! What fire was there in our hall? Go to the front and look at the meditation hall before you speak again.” The monks scrambled to their feet and went to look. Not even the slightest part of the outer doors, windows, or lattice panels of the meditation hall had been scorched. Filled with awe, they now recognized Tripitaka as a divine monk and Wukong as a mighty guardian of the Dharma. Together they came forward and kowtowed, saying, “We had eyes but failed to see, and did not recognize that true immortals had descended to this world. Your cassock is in the rear, with our venerable patriarch in the abbot’s quarters.” Tripitaka passed through three or five stretches of ruined walls and broken masonry, sighing without cease. They saw that the abbot’s quarters had indeed escaped the fire. The monks rushed inside, crying, “Venerable sir, the Tang monk is a divine man and was not burned to death. Instead, we have destroyed our own property. Bring out the cassock at once and return it, so that he may depart.”

p.src: The monks were thrown into a panic and wailed, “Our patriarch has killed himself, and the cassock is missing. What are we to do?” Wukong said, “I expect that one of you has stolen it and hidden it away. All of you, come out and draw up a register of names, so that I may inspect you one by one.” The stewards of the upper and lower quarters drew up two registers listing every monk, mendicant, novice, and lay brother in the monastery, two hundred and thirty persons great and small in all. Wukong asked his master to sit in the place of honor, then called every name from the beginning and searched each person, making them open their robes so that he could examine them plainly. Still there was no cassock. Next he carefully searched from beginning to end all the chests, baskets, and belongings that had been carried from the various quarters during the fire, but not a trace of it could be found. Tripitaka grew distressed at heart and bitterly resented Wukong. Sitting above them, he began to recite the spell. Wukong fell flat to the ground with a thud. Clutching his head, he found the pain almost impossible to bear and cried only, “Do not recite it! Do not recite it! I promise I will find the cassock and return it!” At this sight, every monk trembled with fear. They came forward, knelt, and pleaded with Tripitaka until at last he closed his mouth and ceased reciting. Wukong sprang up in a single bound, drew the iron cudgel from his ear, and was about to strike the monks when Tripitaka shouted him down: “You ape! Are you still not frightened of your headache, that you would behave so outrageously again? Do not use violence or hurt anyone. Question them once more for me.” The monks kowtowed and bowed, pleading mournfully with Tripitaka, “My lord, spare our lives. We truly did not see it. The blame lies entirely with that dead old devil. Last night, after he saw your cassock, he wept until deep into the night. He did not even dare look at it again, but wished to possess it forever and make it an heirloom. So he devised the plot to burn you to death. From the moment the fire broke out, a wild wind raged. Everyone thought only of fighting the flames and carrying possessions to safety, so none of us knows where the cassock went.”

p.src: Sun Wukong flew into a rage. He went into the abbot’s quarters, carried out the body of that wretched old fool who had dashed himself to death, stripped it, and searched it carefully, but the treasure was nowhere on him. He even dug three feet into the ground throughout the abbot’s quarters, but found no trace of it. After pondering for some time, Sun Wukong asked, “Are there any monsters or spirits around here?” The acting abbot replied, “Had you not asked, my lord, you would never have learned of it. Due southeast of here stands Black Wind Mountain. In Black Wind Cave there lives a Black King. That dead old wretch of ours often discussed the Way with him, and he is indeed a monster. There is nothing else of that sort.” Sun Wukong asked, “How far is that mountain from here?” The acting abbot replied, “Only twenty li. That peak you can see over there is the one.” Sun Wukong laughed. “Rest easy, Master. There is no need to say another word. That black monster must have stolen it—there can be no doubt.” Tripitaka said, “His dwelling is twenty li from here. Let old Sun go and seek him out.” Tripitaka said, “If you leave, on whom am I to rely?” Sun Wukong replied, “Do not worry about that. Sun Wukong continued, “Do not merely say yes now and then fail to serve him properly once I am gone. Those attending my master must keep cheerful, pleasant faces; those tending the white horse must give it water and fodder in proper measure. If the slightest thing goes amiss, I shall show you what a cudgel like this can do.” He drew out his cudgel and struck the fire-scorched brick wall with a single crash, smashing it to powder and bringing down another seven or eight courses of wall. At the sight, every monk went weak in the bones and numb in the limbs. Kneeling, kowtowing, and shedding tears, they said, “Grandfather, set your mind at ease and go. We shall exert ourselves with the utmost devotion in attending the reverend master and shall not dare neglect him in the slightest.”
